label: fact:nilpotent
title: Fact
body_md:
\label{fact:nilpotent}
A finite group $G$ is nilpotent if and only if $G$ is the internal direct product of its Sylow
subgroups: $G=P_1\times\cdots\times P_r$, where $p_1,\dots,p_r$ are the distinct primes dividing
$|G|$ and $P_i$ is the (unique, hence normal) Sylow $p_i$-subgroup of $G$.
head: environment
name: Structure of finite nilpotent groups

label: def:splits
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:splits}
A symmetric $S\subseteq G\setminus\{1\}$ splits along the Sylow decomposition if
$S=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^r\iota_i(T_i)$ for symmetric $T_i\subseteq P_i\setminus\{1\}$ with
$\langle T_i\rangle=P_i$.
head: environment

label: lem:regular
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Degree regularity

title: Proof
body_md:
For fixed $v\in P$, $t\mapsto vt$ is an injection $T\to P$ (left multiplication is injective)
whose image is exactly $N(v)=\{w:v^{-1}w\in T\}$, so $\deg(v)=|T|=k$. Summing over $v$ and
applying the handshake lemma gives $|E|=|P|k/2$.
head: environment

label: lem:transreg
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:transreg}
For a connected Cayley graph $\mathrm{Cay}(P,T)$, the transmission $Tr(v):=\sum_ud(v,u)$ is the
same for every $v\in P$, equal to $t:=\sum_{j=1}^{\delta}j\,|T_j|$ ($\delta=\operatorname{diam}$,
$T_j$ its distance layers).
head: environment
name: Transmission regularity

title: Proof
body_md:
Left multiplication $\lambda_g:x\mapsto gx$ is a graph automorphism of any Cayley graph (as
$\lambda_g(x)^{-1}\lambda_g(y)=x^{-1}y$), hence an isometry: $d(gv,gu)=d(v,u)$. So
$Tr(v)=\sum_ud(v,u)=\sum_{u'}d(1,u')=Tr(1)$ (substituting $u=vu'$), giving $Tr\equiv
Tr(1)=\sum_gd(1,g)=t$.
head: environment

label: fact:sumtrans
title: Fact
head: environment
name: Sum of transmissions

title: Proof
body_md:
$\sum_vTr(v)=\sum_v\sum_ud(v,u)$, the sum over all ordered pairs; since $d(v,u)=d(u,v)$ and
$d(v,v)=0$, this equals $2\sum_{\{u,v\}}d(u,v)=2W(\Delta)$.
head: environment

label: lem:cartesian
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cartesian}
$\Gamma\cong\Gamma_1\,\square\cdots\square\,\Gamma_r$: vertex set $\prod_iP_i$, with $(x_i)\sim(y_i)$
iff there is a (necessarily unique) index $i_0$ with $x_{i_0}\ne y_{i_0}$, $x_j=y_j$ for $j\ne
i_0$, and $x_{i_0}^{-1}y_{i_0}\in T_{i_0}$.
head: environment
name: Cartesian product structure

title: Proof
body_md:
Under the direct-product identification, multiplication/inversion in $G$ are componentwise, so
for $x=(x_i),y=(y_i)$, $x^{-1}y=(x_i^{-1}y_i)_i$; this lies in $S=\bigsqcup_i\iota_i(T_i)$ iff it
equals $\iota_{i_0}(s)$ for a unique $i_0$ and some $s\in T_{i_0}$, i.e.\ iff $x_j=y_j$ for
$j\ne i_0$ and $x_{i_0}^{-1}y_{i_0}=s\in T_{i_0}$ — the Cartesian product adjacency rule. In
particular each edge of $\Gamma$ has a well-defined direction $i_0$.
head: environment

label: lem:distadd
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Distance additivity

title: Proof
body_md:
Each edge of $\Gamma$ changes exactly one coordinate (Lemma~\ref{lem:cartesian}), by an edge of
the corresponding factor. In any walk from $(x_i)$ to $(y_i)$, the steps of direction $i$,
projected onto coordinate $i$, form a walk in $\Gamma_i$ from $x_i$ to $y_i$, so there are at
least $d_{\Gamma_i}(x_i,y_i)$ of them; summing over $i$ (steps of different directions being
disjoint), the walk has length at least $\sum_id_{\Gamma_i}(x_i,y_i)$. Concatenating, for
$i=1,\dots,r$, a shortest $\Gamma_i$-path from $x_i$ to $y_i$ (other coordinates fixed) realizes
this bound.
head: environment

label: fact:regrep
title: Fact
body_md:
\label{fact:regrep}
The right regular representation $R$ of $P$ on $\mathbb C[P]$, $(R(g)v)(x)=v(xg)$, decomposes as
$\bigoplus_{\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(P)}V_\chi^{\oplus\chi(1)}$ (Artin--Wedderburn; see
Serre~\cite{Serre1977}, Isaacs~\cite{Isaacs1994}).
head: environment
name: Regular representation

label: lem:diagonalize-nonab
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:diagonalize-nonab}
For a class function $f:P\to\mathbb C$, $z_f:=\sum_gf(g)g$, $M:=R(z_f)$ (so
$M_{x,y}=f(x^{-1}y)$): the eigenvalues of $M$ are $\{\chi(f)/\chi(1):\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(P)\}$
($\chi(f):=\sum_gf(g)\chi(g)$), with multiplicity $\chi(1)^2$.
head: environment
name: Diagonalization by class functions

title: Proof
body_md:
$z_f$ is central (its coefficients are constant on conjugacy classes). By
Fact~\ref{fact:regrep}, $z_f$ acts on each copy of $V_\chi$ inside $R$ as a scalar $\eta_\chi$
(Schur's Lemma), with $\chi(1)\eta_\chi=\operatorname{tr}\rho_\chi(z_f)=\chi(f)$, so
$\eta_\chi=\chi(f)/\chi(1)$, occurring on $\chi(1)$ copies of the $\chi(1)$-dimensional $V_\chi$.
head: environment

label: fact:orthgen
title: Fact
head: environment
name: First Orthogonality Relation

label: lem:chiP
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Vanishing of nontrivial characters

title: Proof
head: environment

label: lem:normal-layers
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Normality propagates to layers

title: Proof
body_md:
Conjugation $c_h$ is a graph automorphism when $T$ is normal ($c_h(x)^{-1}c_h(y)=h(x^{-1}y)h^{-1}$),
fixes $1$, hence preserves each $T_j$ setwise as a bijection of $P$ preserving the finite
partition $\{T_j\}\cup\{\{1\}\}$.
head: environment

label: lem:irr-product
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:irr-product}
Let $\rho_i$ afford $\chi_i\in\mathrm{Irr}(P_i)$ for $i=1,\dots,r$. The external tensor product
$\rho_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_r$, acting on $V_{\chi_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes V_{\chi_r}$ by
$(g_1,\dots,g_r)\mapsto\rho_1(g_1)\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_r(g_r)$, is an irreducible
representation of $G=P_1\times\cdots\times P_r$, with character
$\chi_{\vec\chi}(g_1,\dots,g_r)=\prod_i\chi_i(g_i)$ and degree $\prod_i\chi_i(1)$. As
$(\chi_1,\dots,\chi_r)$ ranges over $\mathrm{Irr}(P_1)\times\cdots\times\mathrm{Irr}(P_r)$, these exhaust
$\mathrm{Irr}(G)$, with no repetitions.
head: environment
name: $\Irr(G)=\Irr(P_1)\otimes\cdots\otimes\Irr(P_r)$

title: Proof
body_md:
That $\rho_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_r$ is a representation of $G$ (a homomorphism into
$GL(V_{\chi_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes V_{\chi_r})$) is immediate, as each factor acts only on its
own tensor slot and the $P_i$ commute elementwise in $G$. Its character is the stated product,
since the trace of a tensor product of operators is the product of their traces.

\emph{Irreducibility and pairwise orthogonality.} For two tuples $\vec\chi=(\chi_1,\dots,\chi_r)$,
$\vec\chi\,'=(\chi_1',\dots,\chi_r')$,
\[
\langle\chi_{\vec\chi},\chi_{\vec\chi\,'}\rangle_G=\frac1{|G|}\sum_{(g_i)}\prod_i\chi_i(g_i)
\overline{\chi_i'(g_i)}=\prod_{i=1}^r\left(\frac1{n_i}\sum_{g_i}\chi_i(g_i)\overline{\chi_i'(g_i)}
\right)=\prod_{i=1}^r\langle\chi_i,\chi_i'\rangle_{P_i}=\prod_{i=1}^r\delta_{\chi_i,\chi_i'},
\]
using $|G|=\prod n_i$ and Fact~\ref{fact:orthgen} on each factor. This product of Kronecker
deltas is $1$ if $\vec\chi=\vec\chi\,'$ (termwise) and $0$ otherwise. Taking $\vec\chi\,'=\vec\chi$:
$\langle\chi_{\vec\chi},\chi_{\vec\chi}\rangle_G=1$, which (a character of norm $1$ is
irreducible) proves irreducibility; taking $\vec\chi\,'\ne\vec\chi$ gives orthogonality, in
particular distinctness (non-isomorphism) of the representations for distinct tuples.

\emph{Completeness.} Summing squared degrees over all tuples,
\[
\sum_{(\chi_1,\dots,\chi_r)}\Big(\prod_i\chi_i(1)\Big)^2=\prod_{i=1}^r\Big(\sum_{\chi_i\in\mathrm{Irr}(P_i)}
\chi_i(1)^2\Big)=\prod_{i=1}^rn_i=|G|,
\]
using $\sum_{\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(P)}\chi(1)^2=|P|$ on each factor (standard: the sum of squared degrees
of all irreducibles of a finite group equals the group order). Since the representations
$\{\rho_{\vec\chi}\}$ are pairwise non-isomorphic and their squared degrees already sum to
$|G|$, no further irreducible representations of $G$ can exist; they exhaust $\mathrm{Irr}(G)$.
head: environment

label: thm:full-spectrum
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:full-spectrum}
For each tuple $\vec\chi=(\chi_1,\dots,\chi_r)\in\mathrm{Irr}(P_1)\times\cdots\times\mathrm{Irr}(P_r)$, let
$Z(\vec\chi):=\{i:\chi_i\ne\chi_0^{(i)}\}$ (the trivial-character complement). Define
\[
\mathcal D(\vec\chi):=\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^rt_i\prod_{j\ne i}n_j=:t & Z(\vec\chi)=\varnothing,\\[3mm]
\displaystyle\Big(\prod_{j\ne i_0}n_j\Big)\,\partial_{\chi_{i_0}}^{(i_0)} & Z(\vec\chi)=\{i_0\},\\[3mm]
0 & |Z(\vec\chi)|\ge2.
\end{cases}
\]
Then
\[
\operatorname{spec}\big(D(\Gamma)\big)=\Big\{\mathcal D(\vec\chi):\vec\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(P_1)\times
\cdots\times\mathrm{Irr}(P_r)\Big\},
\]
with $\mathcal D(\vec\chi)$ occurring with multiplicity $\prod_i\chi_i(1)^2$ (multiplicities of
tuples giving the same numerical value are added).
head: environment
name: Full distance spectrum

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:irr-product}, the representation $\rho_{\vec\chi}=\rho_{\chi_1}\otimes\cdots
\otimes\rho_{\chi_r}$ ranges over all of $\mathrm{Irr}(G)$ as $\vec\chi$ ranges over
$\mathrm{Irr}(P_1)\times\cdots\times\mathrm{Irr}(P_r)$, with degree $\prod_i\chi_i(1)$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:diagonalize-nonab} (applied to $G$ and $f$), $D(\Gamma)=R(z_f)$ acts on (each
copy of) $\rho_{\vec\chi}$ as the scalar $\chi_{\vec\chi}(f)/\chi_{\vec\chi}(1)$, with
multiplicity $\chi_{\vec\chi}(1)^2=\big(\prod_i\chi_i(1)\big)^2=\prod_i\chi_i(1)^2$. It remains to
compute this scalar and show it equals $\mathcal D(\vec\chi)$ as defined.

Equivalently (and more directly), we compute $\rho_{\vec\chi}(z_f)$ using the decomposition
$z_f=\sum_iz_{f_i}^{(i)}\otimes\bigotimes_{j\ne i}z_{\mathbf1}^{(j)}$ derived above. Since
$\rho_{\vec\chi}=\rho_{\chi_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_{\chi_r}$ acts on each tensor factor
$\mathbb C[P_j]$ through $\rho_{\chi_j}$,
\[
\rho_{\vec\chi}(z_f)=\sum_{i=1}^r\rho_{\chi_i}(z_{f_i}^{(i)})\otimes\bigotimes_{j\ne i}
\rho_{\chi_j}(z_{\mathbf1}^{(j)}).
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:diagonalize-nonab} (applied within $P_i$ to $f=f_i$),
$\rho_{\chi_i}(z_{f_i}^{(i)})=\partial_{\chi_i}^{(i)}\,I$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:diagonalize-nonab}
applied within $P_j$ to $f=\mathbf1_{P_j}$ (the constant function $1$), together with
Lemma~\ref{lem:chiP}, $\rho_{\chi_j}(z_{\mathbf1}^{(j)})=\frac{\chi_j(P_j)}{\chi_j(1)}I=n_jI$ if
$\chi_j=\chi_0^{(j)}$, and $=0\cdot I$ if $\chi_j\ne\chi_0^{(j)}$. So the $i$-th summand is the
scalar
\[
\partial_{\chi_i}^{(i)}\cdot\prod_{j\ne i}\big(n_j\,[\chi_j=\chi_0^{(j)}]\big)
=\partial_{\chi_i}^{(i)}\Big(\prod_{j\ne i}n_j\Big)\cdot\Big[\forall j\ne i:\chi_j=\chi_0^{(j)}\Big],
\]
which is zero unless every $\chi_j$ with $j\ne i$ is trivial. Summing over $i=1,\dots,r$:

\emph{Case 1. $Z(\vec\chi)=\varnothing$} (every $\chi_i$ trivial): every summand's indicator holds
(vacuously true condition), giving total $\sum_i\partial_{\chi_0^{(i)}}^{(i)}\prod_{j\ne i}n_j
=\sum_it_i\prod_{j\ne i}n_j=t$.

\emph{Case 2. $Z(\vec\chi)=\{i_0\}$} (exactly one nontrivial, at index $i_0$): for $i=i_0$, the
condition "$\forall j\ne i_0:\chi_j=\chi_0^{(j)}$" holds (as every $j\ne i_0$ is not in
$Z(\vec\chi)$), giving summand $\partial_{\chi_{i_0}}^{(i_0)}\prod_{j\ne i_0}n_j$; for any $i\ne
i_0$, the condition requires $\chi_{i_0}=\chi_0^{(i_0)}$ (as $i_0\ne i$, so $i_0$ is among the
"$j\ne i$" indices to check), which fails since $i_0\in Z(\vec\chi)$; so that summand is $0$.
Total: $\big(\prod_{j\ne i_0}n_j\big)\partial_{\chi_{i_0}}^{(i_0)}$.

\emph{Case 3. $|Z(\vec\chi)|\ge2$}: fix any $i\in\{1,\dots,r\}$; since $|Z(\vec\chi)|\ge2$, there is
some $i_1\in Z(\vec\chi)$ with $i_1\ne i$ (at most one element of $Z(\vec\chi)$ can equal $i$).
Then $\chi_{i_1}\ne\chi_0^{(i_1)}$ with $i_1\ne i$, so the condition "$\forall j\ne i:
\chi_j=\chi_0^{(j)}$" fails (violated at $j=i_1$), making the $i$-th summand $0$. As $i$ was
arbitrary, every summand vanishes: total $0$.

In every case, $\rho_{\vec\chi}(z_f)=\mathcal D(\vec\chi)\,I$, confirming the eigenvalue on
$\rho_{\vec\chi}$ (multiplicity $\prod_i\chi_i(1)^2$) is exactly $\mathcal D(\vec\chi)$, proving
the theorem.
head: environment

label: cor:DL-DQ
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:DL-DQ}
$\Gamma$ is transmission-regular with transmission $t=\sum_it_i\prod_{j\ne i}n_j$ (the
$Z(\vec\chi)=\varnothing$ value of Theorem~\ref{thm:full-spectrum}), so $D^L(\Gamma)=tI-D(\Gamma)$
and $D^Q(\Gamma)=tI+D(\Gamma)$, giving
\[
\operatorname{spec}\big(D^L(\Gamma)\big)=\Big\{t-\mathcal D(\vec\chi):\vec\chi\Big\},\qquad
\operatorname{spec}\big(D^Q(\Gamma)\big)=\Big\{t+\mathcal D(\vec\chi):\vec\chi\Big\},
\]
with the same multiplicities $\prod_i\chi_i(1)^2$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm:full-spectrum}.
Explicitly: the tuple $\vec\chi=(\chi_0^{(1)},\dots,\chi_0^{(r)})$ contributes the eigenvalue $0$
to $D^L(\Gamma)$ (resp.\ $2t$ to $D^Q(\Gamma)$), with multiplicity $1$; every tuple with
$|Z(\vec\chi)|\ge2$ contributes $t$ to $D^L(\Gamma)$ (resp.\ $t$ to $D^Q(\Gamma)$); and every
tuple with $Z(\vec\chi)=\{i_0\}$ contributes $t-\big(\prod_{j\ne i_0}n_j\big)\partial_{\chi_{i_0}}^{(i_0)}$
to $D^L(\Gamma)$ (resp.\ $t+\big(\prod_{j\ne i_0}n_j\big)\partial_{\chi_{i_0}}^{(i_0)}$ to $D^Q(\Gamma)$).
head: environment
name: Full $D^L$ and $D^Q$ spectra

title: Proof
body_md:
Transmission regularity of $\Gamma$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:transreg} applied to $G$) identifies $t$ with
$Tr(1)$, which is exactly the $D(\Gamma)$-eigenvalue on the all-trivial tuple (as computed in
Theorem~\ref{thm:full-spectrum}'s first case) since that eigenvalue's eigenvector is the all-ones
vector of $G$ (the tensor product of the all-ones vectors of each $P_i$, which spans the
$1$-dimensional trivial-tuple isotypic component). Given $D^L=tI-D$, $D^Q=tI+D$, their
eigenvalues are $t\mp\mathcal D(\vec\chi)$ respectively, applied termwise to
Theorem~\ref{thm:full-spectrum}'s formula; the three displayed special cases substitute the three
cases of $\mathcal D(\vec\chi)$ directly.
head: environment

label: ex:main
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:main}
Let $G=Q_8\times\mathbb Z_5$ ($P_1=Q_8$, $n_1=8$; $P_2=\mathbb Z_5$, $n_2=5$; $n=40$), with
$T_1=Q_8\setminus\{1\}$ (so $\Gamma_1=K_8$, $\delta_1=1$) and $T_2=\{1,4\}$ (so
$\Gamma_2=C_5$, $\delta_2=2$).

\emph{Factor $1$ ($K_8$):} $\mathrm{Irr}(Q_8)$ has four linear characters $\chi_0,\chi_a,\chi_b,\chi_{ab}$
(degree $1$) and one degree-$2$ character $\theta$. Since $\Gamma_1=K_8$ has $\delta_1=1$
(single layer $T_1^{(1)}=T_1=Q_8\setminus\{1\}$), $\partial_\chi^{(1)}=\chi(T_1)/\chi(1)$: for the
trivial character, $\chi_0(T_1)=7$, so $\partial_{\chi_0}^{(1)}=7=t_1$; for any nontrivial linear
character $\chi\in\{\chi_a,\chi_b,\chi_{ab}\}$, $\chi(T_1)=\chi(Q_8)-\chi(1)=0-1=-1$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:chiP}), so $\partial_\chi^{(1)}=-1$; for $\theta$, $\theta(T_1)=\theta(Q_8)-\theta(1)
=0-2=-2$, so $\partial_\theta^{(1)}=-2/2=-1$. (All nontrivial eigenvalues of $D(K_8)=J-I$ equal
$-1$, as expected: $K_8$'s distance matrix is $J-I$, with eigenvalues $7$ (once) and $-1$
(seven-fold), matching $1+3+3=7$ dimensions from $\chi_a,\chi_b,\chi_{ab},\theta$ (with
multiplicity $2^2=4$) summing to $1+1+1+4=7$.)

\emph{Factor $2$ ($C_5$):} $\mathrm{Irr}(\mathbb Z_5)=\{\chi_0,\chi_1,\chi_2,\chi_3,\chi_4\}$,
$\chi_k(x)=\zeta_5^{kx}$. With $\delta_2=2$, $T_2^{(1)}=\{1,4\}$, $T_2^{(2)}=\{2,3\}$:
$\partial_{\chi_0}^{(2)}=1\cdot2+2\cdot2=6=t_2$; for $\chi_k$, $k\ne0$,
$\partial_{\chi_k}^{(2)}=(\zeta_5^k+\zeta_5^{4k})+2(\zeta_5^{2k}+\zeta_5^{3k})=2\cos(2\pi k/5)+
4\cos(4\pi k/5)$, giving (using $\cos(2\pi/5)=\frac{\sqrt5-1}4$, $\cos(4\pi/5)=-\frac{\sqrt5+1}4$)
$\partial_{\chi_1}^{(2)}=\partial_{\chi_4}^{(2)}=\frac{\sqrt5-1}2-(\sqrt5+1)=\frac{-\sqrt5-3}2$, and
$\partial_{\chi_2}^{(2)}=\partial_{\chi_3}^{(2)}=-\frac{\sqrt5+1}2+(\sqrt5-1)=\frac{\sqrt5-3}2$.

\emph{Assembling $\operatorname{spec}(D(\Gamma))$ via Theorem~\ref{thm:full-spectrum}}
($n_1=8,n_2=5$, $n=40$; $\mathrm{Irr}(Q_8)=\{\chi_0,\chi_a,\chi_b,\chi_{ab},\theta\}$ of degrees
$1,1,1,1,2$, $\mathrm{Irr}(\mathbb Z_5)=\{\chi_0,\chi_1,\chi_2,\chi_3,\chi_4\}$, all degree $1$):
\begin{itemize}
\item $Z(\vec\chi)=\varnothing$ (the tuple $(\chi_0,\chi_0)$): eigenvalue
$t=t_1n_2+t_2n_1=7\cdot5+6\cdot8=83$, multiplicity $1^2\cdot1^2=1$.
\item $Z(\vec\chi)=\{1\}$ ($P_2$-component trivial): the four tuples
$(\chi_a,\chi_0),(\chi_b,\chi_0),(\chi_{ab},\chi_0),(\theta,\chi_0)$ all give the \emph{same}
eigenvalue $n_2\cdot\partial_\chi^{(1)}=5\cdot(-1)=-5$ (as $\partial_\chi^{(1)}=-1$ for every
nontrivial $\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(Q_8)$, computed above); their multiplicities
$1^2,1^2,1^2,2^2$ sum to $1+1+1+4=7$.
\item $Z(\vec\chi)=\{2\}$ ($P_1$-component trivial): the tuples $(\chi_0,\chi_1)$ and
$(\chi_0,\chi_4)$ give eigenvalue $n_1\partial_{\chi_1}^{(2)}=8\cdot\frac{-\sqrt5-3}2=-4\sqrt5-12$,
total multiplicity $1+1=2$; the tuples $(\chi_0,\chi_2)$ and $(\chi_0,\chi_3)$ give eigenvalue
$n_1\partial_{\chi_2}^{(2)}=8\cdot\frac{\sqrt5-3}2=4\sqrt5-12$, total multiplicity $1+1=2$.
\item $|Z(\vec\chi)|\ge2$ (both components nontrivial): eigenvalue $0$, with multiplicity
$\big(\sum_{\chi\ne\chi_0}\chi(1)^2\big)\cdot\big(\#\{\chi_k:k\ne0\}\big)=(1+1+1+4)\cdot4=28$
(every nontrivial $\mathrm{Irr}(Q_8)$-degree-squared, times the $4$ nontrivial choices in $\mathrm{Irr}(\mathbb
Z_5)$).
\end{itemize}
As a check, the multiplicities sum to $1+7+2+2+28=40=n$, as required.

By Corollary~\ref{cor:DL-DQ} (with $t=83$), the distance Laplacian spectrum is
\[
\{0^{(1)}\}\cup\{88^{(7)}\}\cup\{95+4\sqrt5^{\,(2)}\}\cup\{95-4\sqrt5^{\,(2)}\}\cup\{83^{(28)}\}
\]
(superscripts denoting multiplicities), and the distance signless Laplacian spectrum is
\[
\{166^{(1)}\}\cup\{78^{(7)}\}\cup\{71-4\sqrt5^{\,(2)}\}\cup\{71+4\sqrt5^{\,(2)}\}\cup\{83^{(28)}\}.
\]
Neither is integral (the $\pm4\sqrt5$ terms survive), consistent with $\Gamma_2=C_5$ not being an
integral Cayley graph, since $T_2=\{1,4\}$ is not $\Phi$-invariant for $\mathbb Z_5$ (its
multiplier orbit under $(\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z)^\times$ is all of $\{1,2,3,4\}$, not $\{1,4\}$).
head: environment

label: lem:perron
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:perron}
For $P$ finite, $T\subseteq P\setminus\{1\}$ symmetric, normal, generating, $\Delta=\mathrm{Cay}(P,T)$:
the transmission $t_\Delta$ is the \emph{largest} eigenvalue of $D(\Delta)$, and occurs with
multiplicity exactly $1$.
head: environment
name: Simplicity of the extremal eigenvalue

title: Proof
body_md:
$D(\Delta)$ is a real symmetric matrix with zero diagonal and strictly positive off-diagonal
entries (distinct vertices are at distance $\ge1$), hence an irreducible nonnegative matrix. The
all-ones vector $\mathbf1$ satisfies $D(\Delta)\mathbf1=t_\Delta\mathbf1$ (each row sums to the
transmission) and is strictly positive. By the Perron--Frobenius theorem, an irreducible
nonnegative matrix has a unique (up to scaling) positive eigenvector, and its eigenvalue is both
the spectral radius and simple; since $\mathbf1$ is such a positive eigenvector, $t_\Delta$ is
exactly this eigenvalue: the largest eigenvalue of $D(\Delta)$, occurring with multiplicity $1$.
head: environment

label: cor:simple
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Immediate from Lemma~\ref{lem:perron} applied to $\Delta=\Gamma$ (a Cayley graph on $G$, with
$S$ generating as $\bigsqcup_i\iota_i(T_i)$ is; note this is independent of, and consistent with,
the $Z(\vec\chi)=\varnothing$ case of Theorem~\ref{thm:full-spectrum}, which identifies $t$ as
exactly the eigenvalue attached to the all-trivial tuple — the unique tuple whose eigenvector is
$\mathbf1$). Since $D^L=tI-D$, the eigenvalue $t-t=0$ (attached to the top eigenvalue of $D$)
becomes the \emph{smallest} eigenvalue of $D^L$ (as $D^L$'s eigenvalues are $t$ minus those
of $D$, order reversed), with the same multiplicity $1$; similarly $D^Q=tI+D$ has largest
eigenvalue $t+t=2t$, multiplicity $1$.
head: environment

label: thm:exact-gap
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:exact-gap}
Let
\[
\Lambda:=\min\Big(\big\{t : r\ge2\big\}\cup\Big\{t-\big(\textstyle\prod_{j\ne i}n_j\big)M_i^+ :
i=1,\dots,r\Big\}\Big).
\]
Then $\Lambda$ is exactly the smallest positive eigenvalue of $D^L(\Gamma)$: $(0,\Lambda)$ is a
$D^L$-eigenvalue-free interval, and this is sharp (there is a genuine $D^L(\Gamma)$-eigenvalue
equal to $\Lambda$).
head: environment
name: $D^L$ eigenvalue-free interval

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem~\ref{thm:full-spectrum} and $D^L=tI-D$, the nonzero eigenvalues of $D^L(\Gamma)$ are
exactly $\{t\}$ (if $r\ge2$, from the $|Z(\vec\chi)|\ge2$ case — nonempty precisely when $r\ge2$,
since at least two indices are needed) together with $\big\{t-(\prod_{j\ne i}n_j)\partial_\chi^{(i)}:
i=1,\dots,r,\ \chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(P_i)\setminus\{\chi_0^{(i)}\}\big\}$ (from the $Z(\vec\chi)=\{i\}$
cases). For fixed $i$, since $\prod_{j\ne i}n_j>0$, the quantity $t-(\prod_{j\ne i}n_j)\partial_\chi^{(i)}$
is minimized over $\chi\ne\chi_0^{(i)}$ exactly when $\partial_\chi^{(i)}$ is maximized, i.e.\ at
$\partial_\chi^{(i)}=M_i^+$ (attained, as the max of a finite nonempty set), giving minimum value
$t-(\prod_{j\ne i}n_j)M_i^+$. Taking the overall minimum over $i$ and, if applicable, including
$t$, gives exactly $\Lambda$ as the minimum of the whole nonzero part of the spectrum — i.e.\ the
smallest positive eigenvalue — and this value is attained (by construction, as a minimum over a
finite set of values each individually attained).
head: environment

label: thm:exact-gap-Q
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:exact-gap-Q}
Let
\[
\Lambda':=\max\Big(\big\{t : r\ge2\big\}\cup\Big\{t+\big(\textstyle\prod_{j\ne i}n_j\big)M_i^+ :
i=1,\dots,r\Big\}\Big).
\]
Then $\Lambda'$ is exactly the largest eigenvalue of $D^Q(\Gamma)$ strictly below $2t$:
$(\Lambda',2t)$ is a $D^Q$-eigenvalue-free interval, sharp in the same sense.
head: environment
name: $D^Q$ eigenvalue-free interval

title: Proof
body_md:
Identical to Theorem~\ref{thm:exact-gap}, using $D^Q=tI+D$: the sub-Perron eigenvalues are
$\{t\}$ (if $r\ge2$) and $\{t+(\prod_{j\ne i}n_j)\partial_\chi^{(i)}\}$, each of the latter
maximized (for fixed $i$) at $\partial_\chi^{(i)}=M_i^+$, giving the stated maximum $\Lambda'$ as
the largest sub-Perron eigenvalue.
head: environment

label: lem:triangle
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:triangle}
$M_i^+\le t_i$ for every $i$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For any $\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(P_i)$ and $g\in P_i$, $|\chi(g)|\le\chi(1)$ (the character value is a sum of
$\chi(1)$ roots of unity, each of modulus $1$, so the triangle inequality gives
$|\chi(g)|\le\chi(1)$). Hence, for each layer, $|\chi(T_i^{(k)})|=\big|\sum_{g\in
T_i^{(k)}}\chi(g)\big|\le\sum_{g\in T_i^{(k)}}|\chi(g)|\le|T_i^{(k)}|\chi(1)$, so
\[
|\partial_\chi^{(i)}|=\frac1{\chi(1)}\Big|\sum_{k=1}^{\delta_i}k\,\chi(T_i^{(k)})\Big|
\le\frac1{\chi(1)}\sum_{k=1}^{\delta_i}k\,|T_i^{(k)}|\chi(1)=\sum_{k=1}^{\delta_i}k\,|T_i^{(k)}|=t_i.
\]
In particular $\partial_\chi^{(i)}\le t_i$ for every $\chi$, so $M_i^+\le t_i$.
head: environment

label: cor:nonneg
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:nonneg}
$\Lambda\ge0$ and $\Lambda'\le2t$; equivalently, $D^L(\Gamma)$ is positive semidefinite and every
eigenvalue of $D^Q(\Gamma)$ lies in $[0,2t]$ — proved here directly from
Lemma~\ref{lem:triangle}, without invoking positive-semidefiniteness of $D^L$ as an external fact.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:triangle}, for every $i$,
\[
t-\Big(\prod_{j\ne i}n_j\Big)M_i^+\ \ge\ t-\Big(\prod_{j\ne i}n_j\Big)t_i
=\sum_{k\ne i}t_k\prod_{l\ne k}n_l\ \ge\ 0,
\]
the last step as a sum of nonnegative terms ($t_k\ge0$ always, being a sum of nonnegative
distances). Also $t\ge0$ trivially. Hence $\Lambda\ge0$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:exact-gap}, a minimum of
nonnegative quantities). The bound $\Lambda'\le2t$ follows symmetrically: $t+(\prod_{j\ne
i}n_j)M_i^+\le t+(\prod_{j\ne i}n_j)t_i=2t-\sum_{k\ne i}t_k\prod_{l\ne k}n_l\le2t$, and $t\le2t$
trivially (as $t\ge0$).
head: environment

label: rem:not-sharp
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:not-sharp}
Corollary~\ref{cor:nonneg} only recovers $\Lambda\ge0$: it does \emph{not}, on its own, establish
a strictly positive universal gap (of a fixed size such as $n$) below which $D^L(\Gamma)$
provably has no nonzero eigenvalues, for arbitrary $\Gamma$. A sharp universal bound of that
general form is known in the literature for the \emph{second-largest} distance Laplacian
eigenvalue of a general graph (ordering eigenvalues $\partial_1^L\ge\partial_2^L\ge\cdots\ge
\partial_n^L=0$, one has $\partial_2^L(G)\ge n$, with equality iff $G\cong K_n$ or $K_n-e$; see
the surveys~\cite{RatherAouchiche2025,RatherGanieWang2026}); but that quantity bounds
$\partial_1^L,\partial_2^L$ near the \emph{top} of the spectrum, and is logically distinct from
the smallest nonzero eigenvalue $\Lambda=\partial_{n-1}^L$ near the \emph{bottom}, which is a
separately studied invariant and does not, to our knowledge, admit an analogous universal bound
in the literature. Theorems~\ref{thm:exact-gap} and~\ref{thm:exact-gap-Q} give the exact value of
$\Lambda,\Lambda'$ instead, for the nilpotent-group Cayley graph family, which is the strongest
correct statement available from the tools developed here.
head: environment

label: cor:integral-gap
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:integral-gap}
Suppose every $\Gamma_i$ is distance-integral (i.e.\ $\partial_\chi^{(i)}\in\mathbb Z$ for every
$\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(P_i)$ and every $i$). Then $\Lambda\ge1$ and $\Lambda'\le2t-1$: that is, $(0,1)$ is
$D^L$-eigenvalue-free and $(2t-1,2t)$ is $D^Q$-eigenvalue-free — in fact $D^L(\Gamma)$ and
$D^Q(\Gamma)$ are then themselves fully integral matrices, so every nonzero $D^L$-eigenvalue is a
positive integer and every sub-Perron $D^Q$-eigenvalue is an integer at most $2t-1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If every $\partial_\chi^{(i)}\in\mathbb Z$, then every term in the spectrum formula for
$D(\Gamma)$ ($t$, $0$, and $(\prod_{j\ne i}n_j)\partial_\chi^{(i)}$, all built from integers) is an
integer, so $D(\Gamma)$, hence $D^L(\Gamma)=tI-D(\Gamma)$ and $D^Q(\Gamma)=tI+D(\Gamma)$
($t\in\mathbb Z$ automatically), are integral matrices. By Corollary~\ref{cor:simple}, $0$ is the
strictly smallest $D^L(\Gamma)$-eigenvalue with multiplicity $1$; the next-smallest, $\Lambda$
(Theorem~\ref{thm:exact-gap}), is therefore a \emph{positive} integer, i.e.\ $\Lambda\ge1$. The
$D^Q$ statement is symmetric, using $2t$ as the strictly largest, simple eigenvalue
(Corollary~\ref{cor:simple}) and $\Lambda'$ as the next-largest.
head: environment

label: ex:gap
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:gap}
Continuing Example~\ref{ex:main} ($G=Q_8\times\mathbb Z_5$, $n_1=8,n_2=5,n=40$, $t_1=7,t_2=6,t=83$):
there $\partial_\chi^{(1)}=-1$ for every nontrivial $\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(Q_8)$, so $M_1^+=-1$, and
$\partial_{\chi_k}^{(2)}\in\big\{\frac{-\sqrt5-3}2,\frac{\sqrt5-3}2\big\}$ for $k=1,2,3,4$, so
$M_2^+=\frac{\sqrt5-3}2$ (the larger of the two, at $k=2,3$).

By Theorem~\ref{thm:exact-gap} ($r=2$, so $t=83$ is a candidate):
\[
t-\Big(\prod_{j\ne1}n_j\Big)M_1^+=83-5\cdot(-1)=88,\qquad
t-\Big(\prod_{j\ne2}n_j\Big)M_2^+=83-8\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt5-3}2=83-4\sqrt5+12=95-4\sqrt5\approx86.06.
\]
So $\Lambda=\min(83,\,88,\,95-4\sqrt5)=83$ (the $|Z(\vec\chi)|\ge2$ case itself, which is here the
smallest of the three candidates) — matching the distance Laplacian spectrum computed in
Example~\ref{ex:main}, $\{0,88^{(7)},95\pm4\sqrt5\,{}^{(2)},83^{(28)}\}$, whose smallest nonzero
value is indeed $83$. Since $\Gamma_2=C_5$ is not distance-integral (its nontrivial eigenvalues
involve $\sqrt5$), Corollary~\ref{cor:integral-gap} does not apply here — consistent with
$\Lambda=83$ not being forced to any particular integer threshold beyond what is computed exactly.
head: environment
